newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: President says no Bangui unity government for now.
newsitem.headline: President says no Bangui unity government for now.

text.p: Central African Republic's president has said he will form a new government shortly but without the opposition -- a key provision of an African mediated deal to end a cycle of political, military and ethnic violence.

Ange-Felix Patasse told representatives of the impoverished nation's 25 recognised political parties on Wednesday that the opposition had not responded to his outstretched hand but he would form a government anyway.

"I do not want to go into the details of the consultations but before the Central African nation and international opinion I assume my responsibilities and the government will be formed shortly," he said.

The January 25 Bangui Accord, brokered by Mali's widely respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure, was designed to end the country's third army mutiny in under a year and curb ethnic rivalry that had already led to bloodshed.

Troops from Mali, Burkina Faso, Gabon and Chad, whose presidents launched the mediation effort in December at the behest of a Franco-African summit, are in Bangui to replace French troops who have been keeping rival factions apart.
Troops from Senegal and Togo are also part of this force.
Patasse named outgoing foreign minister Michel Gbezzera-Bria on January 30 to head the new government.
"I held out my hand, I appealed for all of us to make a patriotic leap forward to retrieve the situation in the Central African Republic in serenity and fraternity," he said on Wednesday.
"As this is (not) the way it is, I assume my responsibilities under the Central African Republic's constitution," he added.
Political pundits in Bangui predicted a government drawn from Patasse's ruling Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People (MLPC) and four allied parties.
Patasse did not rule out further talks. "I think that we will have other occasions to meet and that the door is not closed, even if I form the government today or tomorrow."
Mutinies in April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a northern civilian who won presidential elections in 1993.
The latest mutiny, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic feuding. The mutineers were from the minority Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
French troops, in the country under a defence pact, stepped in to restore order. Estimates of those killed in the mutinies range from scores to several hundred.
